# Renewal Theory Fluctuations and Applications to Bit-Comparison Random Trees

## Distributional Fluctuations in Renewal Counting Processes

Classical renewal theory typically establishes that the number of renewals up to time $t$, denoted $N(t)$, satisfies a law of large numbers and, under suitable moment conditions, a central limit theorem as $t \to \infty$. However, when the underlying sequence of lifetimes—the inter-renewal times—grows at an exponential rate in a distributional sense, the standard asymptotic behavior breaks down in a striking way. Rather than converging to a fixed distribution (after appropriate centering and scaling), the renewal counting process $N(t)$ exhibits persistent distributional fluctuations as $t \to \infty$. That is, the law of $N(t)$, suitably normalized, does not stabilize to a single limiting distribution but instead oscillates, with the fluctuation pattern depending on the specific manner in which $t$ approaches infinity. This phenomenon arises precisely because the exponential growth rate of the lifetimes disrupts the usual renewal-theoretic scaling, leading to a periodic or quasi-periodic dependence of the limiting behavior on $t$ (or on $\log t$, given the exponential nature of the growth).

## Connection to Random Trees via Bit-Comparison Strategies

This renewal fluctuation phenomenon is not merely a technical curiosity in probability theory—it furnishes a natural and illuminating probabilistic mechanism underlying the asymptotic analysis of insertion depth in a particular class of random tree structures. Specifically, consider random trees built through a bit-comparison strategy, wherein elements are inserted based on comparisons of their binary digit expansions, and the input consists of independent, identically distributed uniform random variables. The depth of insertion in such trees—a fundamental parameter governing the tree's structural complexity and the efficiency of associated algorithms—can be reinterpreted through the lens of a renewal process. In this correspondence, the successive bit-comparisons play the role of renewal epochs, and because the relevant "lifetimes" in this embedded renewal process grow exponentially (reflecting the binary, digit-by-digit nature of the comparisons), the same fluctuation phenomenon documented in the renewal-theoretic setting manifests itself in the asymptotic distribution of the insertion depth. This connection provides deep probabilistic insight into why the insertion depth in bit-comparison trees fails to converge to a single limiting law, instead displaying oscillatory asymptotic behavior tied to the discrete, exponential structure of the underlying binary comparisons.

## Representation of the Limiting Laws

Building on this correspondence, the present study derives an explicit representation for the family of limit laws that arise along appropriate subsequences of $t$ (or of the tree size, in the combinatorial setting). Because the fluctuating behavior precludes convergence along the full continuum of $t$, the natural object of study becomes the collection of subsequential limits, indexed by the fractional part of $\log t$ (or an analogous quantity reflecting the exponential time scale). The representation obtained characterizes this entire family of limiting distributions in a unified analytic framework, capturing both the periodic dependence on the subsequence parameter and the underlying probabilistic structure inherited from the renewal process. This representation thereby serves as a rigorous and comprehensive description of the asymptotic distributional landscape governing insertion depth in bit-comparison random trees.

## Rates of Convergence

Beyond establishing the existence and form of the limiting laws along subsequences, the methodology developed in this work possesses additional analytical strength: it can be extended to yield quantitative rates of convergence for the associated distributional limits. That is, the same techniques used to derive the representation of the limit laws also permit one to control the speed at which the (subsequential) distributions of the renewal counts—and correspondingly, the insertion depths in the random trees—approach their limiting forms. This dual capability, offering both a qualitative characterization of the limiting family and quantitative bounds on the convergence rate, underscores the robustness and versatility of the probabilistic approach undertaken in this study.

# Renewal Processes with Exponentially Growing Lifetimes: Distributional Periodicity and Applications to Digital Trees

## Abstract and Overview

Classical renewal theory establishes that for a sequence of independent, identically distributed positive lifetimes with finite mean, the associated counting process $N(t)$, which records the number of renewals occurring up to time $t$, satisfies a strong law of large numbers and, after appropriate centering and scaling, a central limit theorem as $t \to \infty$. The present study departs from this classical framework by considering renewal processes in which the lifetimes themselves grow exponentially in a distributional sense — that is, the successive interarrival times are stochastically equivalent, after rescaling by a geometric factor, to a fixed reference distribution. This structural feature fundamentally alters the long-time behavior of the counting process: rather than stabilizing around a deterministic growth rate as $t \to \infty$, the (suitably normalized) counting process $N(t)$ fails to converge in distribution. Instead, it exhibits a persistent oscillatory behavior, fluctuating among a continuum — or family — of limiting laws indexed by the fractional part of $\log t$ (with respect to the base governing the exponential growth of the lifetimes).

## Motivation and Context

This phenomenon of distributional non-convergence, sometimes termed "periodic fluctuation" or "distributional oscillation," is a well-documented feature in the probabilistic analysis of digital data structures, most notably in the study of tries, PATRICIA tries, and related bit-comparison-based random trees built from independent uniformly distributed inputs. In such structures, the depth of insertion of a new key — that is, the number of bit comparisons required to locate its position — is known to exhibit fluctuations that do not vanish asymptotically as the number of stored keys grows, but instead persist in the form of small-amplitude oscillations around a logarithmic growth rate. Traditionally, such results have been obtained through analytic combinatorics, via Mellin transform techniques and poles located on vertical lines in the complex plane, which mechanically produce periodic terms but offer comparatively little direct probabilistic insight into their origin.

The renewal-theoretic framework developed here supplies precisely this missing probabilistic explanation. By reinterpreting the process of successive bit comparisons as a renewal process whose lifetimes grow geometrically — reflecting the halving of the effective search space at each level of the tree — one recovers the insertion-depth asymptotics as a direct consequence of the distributional non-convergence of the associated counting process. The oscillatory limiting behavior of the renewal counts thus provides a transparent, coupling- and construction-based account of the periodic fluctuations previously accessible only through singularity analysis.

## Main Contributions

Beyond this explanatory role, the paper makes several concrete technical contributions:

1. **Non-convergence and distributional characterization.** We show rigorously that the counting process $N(t)$, under natural centering and normalization, does not converge in distribution as $t \to \infty$. Instead, along any sequence $t_n \to \infty$, the possible subsequential limits form a one-parameter family of laws.

2. **Representation of the limiting family.** For each value of the limiting fractional part of $\log t$ (with respect to the relevant exponential base), we derive an explicit stochastic representation of the corresponding limit law. This representation is obtained via a fixed-point (recursive distributional) equation that arises naturally from the self-similar, geometric structure of the lifetimes, and it identifies the limit as the solution of a stochastic fixed-point equation reminiscent of those appearing in the analysis of recursive algorithms and branching structures.

3. **Rates of convergence.** Using this representation, together with probabilistic metrics adapted to the recursive structure (such as the Zolotarev or minimal $L^p$-metrics), we establish quantitative bounds on the rate at which the finite-time law of $N(t)$ approaches its corresponding subsequential limit. These rates are shown to be geometric, reflecting the underlying exponential growth of the lifetimes, and they refine previously known qualitative statements of convergence to include explicit error terms.

## Structure of the Paper

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first set up the renewal model with exponentially growing lifetimes and establish basic distributional identities. We then prove the non-convergence result and characterize the family of subsequential limits via a recursive distributional equation. The connection to insertion depth in bit-comparison-based random trees is developed in detail, showing how the renewal-theoretic oscillations translate into the known periodic fluctuation phenomena of digital search trees and tries. Finally, we derive explicit convergence rates using contraction-based coupling arguments, and we discuss extensions of the method to related classes of self-similar random structures.

# This and Our: Reflections on Presence and Belonging

There is something quietly powerful in the words "this" and "our." They are small, unassuming, yet they carry the weight of immediacy and connection.

**This** points to the present moment—to what is here, now, tangible. It is a word of specificity, cutting through abstraction to say: not that, not something distant, but *this*. This conversation. This choice. This breath. When we say "this matters," we are grounding ourselves in the concrete, refusing to let meaning drift into vagueness. "This" demands attention. It insists that whatever it modifies deserves to be seen clearly, examined honestly, and taken seriously.

**Our** does something different—it gathers. It transforms the individual into the collective, the isolated "I" into a shared "we." "Our" speaks of belonging, of shared responsibility, and shared stake. Our home. Our future. Our mistakes. Our hopes. It is a word that resists loneliness, that insists we are not separate from those around us but bound together by common ground, common cause, or common fate.

Together, these words shape how we understand responsibility and presence. To say "this is our moment" is to root a shared identity in a specific instant—to claim ownership not of some abstract ideal, but of something real and immediate. It calls people to act together, right now, rather than deferring to someday or someone else.

In a world that often pulls us toward distraction and division, "this" and "our" offer a quiet corrective. They ask us to notice what is directly in front of us and to remember that we rarely face it alone. Whether in community, family, work, or purpose, these two small words remind us that meaning is found in the specific and the shared—in *this*, and in *our* willingness to hold it together.

# Abstract

We study the asymptotic behavior of insertion depth in tries constructed from independent, identically distributed sequences over a uniform alphabet, establishing a novel connection to renewal theory with exponentially growing interarrival times. By representing the trie insertion process as a sequence of comparisons governed by the binary (or $q$-ary) expansions of uniform random inputs, we show that the depth of insertion can be reformulated as a renewal counting process in which the "lifetimes" between successive renewals grow geometrically due to the recursive halving structure inherent in trie construction. This correspondence allows classical renewal-theoretic tools—including the elementary renewal theorem, Blackwell's theorem, and refined local limit results—to be adapted to a non-standard setting where the increments are not identically distributed but instead scale exponentially with the renewal index.

We derive precise asymptotic expansions for the mean and variance of the insertion depth, recovering and sharpening known results $\mathbb{E}[D_n] = \log_2 n + \text{(periodic fluctuation)} + o(1)$, while providing a unified probabilistic explanation for the characteristic oscillatory behavior observed in trie parameters. Our approach yields a functional limit theorem showing that the fluctuations around the logarithmic growth rate converge to a periodic function of $\log_2 n$ perturbed by fluctuations governed by an associated renewal-type stationary process, and we quantify the rate of convergence via Mellin transform techniques combined with a coupling argument for the exponential renewal scheme.

Beyond recovering first- and second-order asymptotics, we establish a distributional limit theorem: after centering and an appropriate periodic correction, the insertion depth satisfies a central limit theorem with an explicit, non-Gaussian correction term arising from the discrete, self-similar nature of the underlying renewal process. This provides a new probabilistic lens for understanding the source of periodic fluctuations pervasive in the analysis of digital trees, and it suggests that renewal processes with exponentially growing lifetimes constitute a natural and previously underexploited framework for analyzing a broad class of trie-based algorithms, radix sort, and related digital search structures.

# Abstract

We consider a renewal process whose interarrival times are governed by a distribution with exponentially increasing tails, specifically the class of lifetime distributions arising from geometric-like scaling $P(\xi > t) \sim q^t$ for $t \in \mathbb{N}$, $0 < q < 1$, a regime naturally induced by binary (or $b$-ary) digital search trees and tries. Unlike classical renewal theory, where the renewal function grows linearly and satisfies a central limit theorem, the exponential growth of lifetimes forces the counting process $N(t)$—the number of renewals up to time $t$—to grow only logarithmically, $N(t) \sim \log_{1/q} t$, and its fluctuations fail to converge to a single limiting law. Instead, due to periodic oscillations inherited from the discreteness of the lifetime distribution, the normalized counting process $N(t) - \log_{1/q} t$ exhibits *no* overall convergence in distribution; rather, convergence holds only along subsequences $t_n$ for which $\log_{1/q} t_n$ approaches a fixed fractional part.

Each $F_\alpha$ arises as the distribution of a Poissonized or shifted-Poisson-type functional and can be characterized explicitly via its generating function or Laplace transform, expressed in terms of the Mellin transform machinery associated with the harmonic sum representation of the renewal function.

This result illuminates the well-known "asymptotic oscillation" phenomenon pervasive in the analysis of digital data structures: the size, depth, and profile parameters of tries and digital search trees—whose recursive probabilistic structure mirrors exactly this exponential renewal process—exhibit fluctuating rather than smoothly converging limit laws, and the present family $\{F_\alpha\}$ provides the precise probabilistic description of these fluctuations, unifying earlier ad hoc analyses of trie depth and PATRICIA trie parameters under a single renewal-theoretic framework.

# Abstract

We investigate the asymptotic behavior of renewal counting processes N(t) associated with sequences of independent, non-identically distributed nonnegative random variables (lifetimes) satisfying a mild exponential growth condition. Under this condition, we show that the standard central limit theorem fails to hold in the classical sense; instead, the distribution of N(t), suitably centered and normalized, exhibits a persistent oscillatory behavior as t→∞. More precisely, we prove that the sequence of distributions does not converge but instead oscillates between distinct limiting laws along appropriate subsequences, a phenomenon rarely observed in renewal theory and closely tied to the interplay between the growth rate of the lifetime distributions and the discrete lattice structure inherent in many combinatorial applications.

The main theoretical contribution is a precise characterization of this oscillation, including an explicit description of the limiting distributions involved and a quantitative estimate for the rate of convergence of the underlying distributional sequence to its oscillatory limit set, expressed in terms of a suitable probability metric (such as the Wasserstein or Kolmogorov distance). These convergence rate results allow us to control the fluctuations uniformly and provide sharp error bounds that complement the qualitative oscillation phenomenon.

As a key application, we employ this renewal-theoretic framework to analyze the insertion depth in bit-comparison random trees, a fundamental class of digital search structures including tries, PATRICIA tries, and related tree models used in algorithms and data structures. We demonstrate that the depth of a randomly inserted key, when properly normalized, inherits the oscillatory limiting behavior established in our general renewal theorem, rather than converging to a fixed Gaussian or other classical limit law. This resolves a subtlety previously observed only heuristically or numerically in the probabilistic analysis of such trees, and it provides a rigorous explanation for the periodic fluctuations in variance and higher moments that have been reported in the literature on digital trees.

Our approach combines techniques from renewal theory, Fourier/Mellin analysis, and probabilistic combinatorics, and it offers a unified framework applicable to a broader class of problems in the analysis of algorithms where exponential-type lifetime or spacing distributions naturally arise. We discuss the implications of our results for the precise probabilistic analysis of random tree structures and outline directions for extending the oscillation and convergence rate estimates to related models, including generalized tries and other digital search trees with heterogeneous branching probabilities.
